title: Associations of job satisfaction and job stress with personality changes across the retirement transition: A conceptual replication of Schimanski et al. (2026a).
abstract: The workplace is an important context for adult development. Consequently, retiring causes profound shifts in social interactions, daily routines, and personal identity. Nevertheless, there is limited research on how specific work-related factors are related to personality changes, particularly during the retirement transition. The present study is a conceptual replication of Schimanski et al. (2026a) examining associations of preretirement job satisfaction and job stress with Big Five personality trait changes across the retirement transition. Using data from the 2006 to 2016 waves of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), we identified 771 individuals (44-83 years at baseline,= 60.95 years,= 5.59; 60% women) who retired within this period. We additionally identified a propensity-score-matched control group of 771 individuals who continued to work (42-82 years at baseline,= 60.72,= 5.91; 61% women). Multigroup latent change score models were calculated based on the last wave before and first wave after retirement or two consecutive waves of continued employment, respectively, with the two waves being 4 years apart. In both groups, neuroticism decreased significantly, while openness decreased only among retirees. Preretirement job satisfaction and job stress were significantly related to baseline personality trait levels but not to changes. The results are consistent with Schimanski et al. Overall, our findings suggest that retirement has minimal long-term effects on personality, and job satisfaction and job stress do not shape personality changes during this transition. The discussion focuses on implications for future studies regarding methodological approaches and possible predictors of change. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).
